title: Take up your cross (Mark 8:31–38)
hook: Peter rebukes him about suffering, is called Satan, and hears: lose your life to save it

segments.voice: Yesterday, near Caesarea Philippi, Peter called him the Christ. Your line was who do you say I am?

Thou art the Christ. Top of the class. Then, straight away, Jesus starts to explain what that will mean, and none of it is what they hoped to hear. He'll suffer many things. He'll be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. He'll be killed. And after three days he'll rise again. He says it openly, Mark adds. So Peter, like any loyal friend, takes Jesus aside, quietly, and tells him off. No. Not that. Not you. And Jesus turns around, looks at the others, and answers Peter in front of all of them.
screen: `TOP OF THE CLASS.` → `HE MUST SUFFER.` → `PETER TAKES HIM ASIDE.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "Get thee behind me, Satan." From top of the class to Satan in a handful of verses. It sounds brutal. But in Hebrew, satan means an adversary, the one who stands in your way. One way to hear it: Peter has put himself in front of Jesus, blocking the road. Get behind me: go back to following. Then he calls the crowd over, with his disciples: "Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." Today a cross can be a necklace or a steeple. To that crowd it was a Roman way of putting people to death, in public, and as Mark will later show, a cross was carried through the streets to the place of death. The words may well have made them flinch. Then the riddle at the center: "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it." Grip your life too tight and it slips away. Christians have read this in more than one way. For the early church, under persecution, it could mean dying for the faith. Luke's version adds the word daily, and some hear it as ordinary self-giving: the parent up at 3am, the friend who shows up. And some churches today say plainly what it does not mean: it is not a command to stay in harm or abuse. The verse itself holds both halves, side by side: lose, and save.
screen: `FROM TOP OF THE CLASS TO SATAN.` · `SATAN: THE ONE IN THE WAY.` · `A CROSS WAS AN EXECUTION.` · `LOSE IT TO FIND IT.` · then, large: `TAKE UP HIS CROSS, AND FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Think of one person, and what would make their day lighter: your turn to choose the show, the last slice, twenty minutes you'd planned for yourself, something that costs a little, not a lot. Picture yourself handing it over, and notice whether your hands want to hold on. If you pray, you can offer it to God as part of following; if you don't, just decide.
Cross: in Jesus's day, the walk of the condemned; in faith, what it costs to follow him.
Your line: lose it to find it. Behind him, not in his way. See you on the mountain.

howItsDone: Some Christians speak of their own small sacrifices as carrying the cross, and some take on a daily act of self-giving; in Lent especially, churches that keep the season invite people to give something up for the sake of others.

fork.setup: you're Peter. your teacher has just said he will suffer and be killed. you love him. what do you do?
options: take him aside and tell him not to say such things.
say nothing and hope he's wrong.
tell the crowd to protect him.
fork.reveal: Peter rebukes him privately, and Jesus answers him in front of everyone: get thee behind me, Satan. Peter meant love, and still stood in the road.

original.note: Greek: an upright stake, and then the cross Rome used for executions.

trapdoor: what you thought: take up your cross means put up with an annoyance.
what it means: to follow Jesus even when it costs, because life held too tightly is lost and life given is found.
what a scholar hears: the same Greek word, psychē, is life in verse 35 and soul in verse 36. Luke's version adds daily.
recall: what's handed on from one hand to the next
the fringe or tassel on a garment's corner

notes: The rebuke comes four verses after Peter's confession (8:29 to 8:33); the script says 'in five verses' counting inclusively. Confirm or adjust.
The condemned carrying the crossbeam (patibulum) is described as 'often'; confirm.
Psychē as life (8:35) and soul (8:36) in the KJV: confirm the trapdoor claim.
The line that the cross is not a command to stay in harm or abuse reflects the pastoral teaching of many churches; Keeper to confirm the wording is fair and appropriate.
